name: Ibadi Imamate of Oman (Nabhani and Yaruba)
summary: The Ibadi Muslim imamate and sultans of inland Oman; the Yaruba imams drove the Portuguese out of Muscat (1650) and built an Indian Ocean sea power before civil war led to the Al Said dynasty.

location.value: Inner Oman (the region around Nizwa and the Hajar Mountains) and, under the Yaruba, the coast from Muscat to the Gulf of Oman.

terrain.value: The rugged Hajar Mountains, palm-filled oasis valleys (wadis) and a hot coastal plain.

climate.value: Very hot and dry, with rare winter rains and occasional storms from the Arabian Sea.

resources.value: Dates and other oasis crops, copper in the Hajar Mountains, fish, horses for export, and frankincense from the south.

disasters.value: Droughts that dried up wells and aflaj channels; occasional cyclones on the coast.

population.value: Perhaps a few hundred thousand, living in oasis villages and coastal towns.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages and farming land around a royal capital.

disease.value: Malaria in some oases, smallpox and famine after droughts.

migration.value: Omani traders and settlers moved to the East African coast (Mombasa, Zanzibar) after the wars with Portugal.

economicBase.value: Oasis farming watered by aflaj (underground channels), plus fishing and sea trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Indian Ocean routes linking Muscat with India, Persia and East Africa.

wealth.value: Grew rich under the Yaruba imams from sea trade and the ports taken from the Portuguese.

moneyAndTax.value: Foreign silver coins from India and Persia; religious taxes (zakat) and customs on trade.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above farmers; some slavery or bonded labour.

governmentType.value: Ibadi imams chosen by scholars and tribal leaders; between them, the Nabhani dynasty ruled as hereditary kings (about 1154–1624).

keyRulers.value: Nasir bin Murshid (elected 1624), who began the Yaruba imamate; Sultan bin Saif I, who took Muscat from Portugal (1650); Saif bin Sultan I (1692–1711).

succession.value: Imams chosen by scholars; later hereditary.

institutions.value: The imam, Ibadi religious scholars who elected and advised him, and tribal sheikhs.

stability.value: A civil war between rival Yaruba candidates and their tribal backers began in 1719.

eliteConflict.value: Tribes split into two great factions, the Hinawi and the Ghafiri, during the civil war.

armyAndTech.value: Tribal soldiers and a navy of captured and newly built ships armed with cannon; large forts with round towers.

majorWars.value: Drove the Portuguese from Muscat (1650) and fought them along the East African coast, taking Fort Jesus at Mombasa (1698).

territoryChange.value: Took Mombasa (1698) and the Swahili coast.

alliancesRivals.value: Portugal was the main enemy at sea; later the Persians under Nader Shah invaded during the civil war.

inventions.value: No major inventions; the aflaj irrigation channels were a remarkable older technology that Oman maintained.

scienceEducation.value: Ibadi religious scholarship in centres such as Nizwa and Rustaq.

openness.value: Open to Indian Ocean trade, while inner Oman stayed conservative and religious.

communicationTransport.value: Camel and donkey tracks through the mountains; dhows along the coast and across the ocean.

religion.value: Ibadi Islam, a branch of Islam distinct from Sunni and Shia, which is still the main faith in Oman.

artsArchitecture.value: Great forts: Bahla (a World Heritage Site), the round tower of Nizwa and the palace-fort of Jabrin (1670s).

socialStructure.value: The imam and religious scholars, tribal sheikhs, merchants, farmers and fishermen, and enslaved people.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the Ibadi imamate and to tribe; pride in expelling the Portuguese.

dailyLife.value: Families farmed date palms and small fields in oases, sharing aflaj water by a strict timetable.

ideasReligions.value: The Ibadi idea that the community should choose the most worthy imam rather than follow a hereditary king.

riseSignals.value: Nasir bin Murshid was elected imam in 1624, founding the Yaruba line.

peakPeriod.value: After 1650, when the Yaruba became a sea power from Muscat to East Africa.

declineSignals.value: Civil war from 1719 and Persian invasions (1737 and 1743).

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and foreign reports; figures are estimates.
